costGuide.title: Hyundai G4LC Engine Replacement Cost (UK)
costGuide.labourLine: Fitting a G4LC typically takes 7-10 hours at £65-£85/hr (independent) - confirm exact labour when comparing quotes.
paragraphs: What genuinely moves the price for the G4LC is the condition of the timing chain and whether oil consumption has already begun - a well-maintained unit with documented chain history commands a premium, while an engine showing signs of bore wear or high oil consumption is a rebuild candidate rather than a simple recon. The G4LC's aluminium block cannot be overbored if scored - replacement is the only option for cylinder damage. See our full reconditioned engine cost guide

failures.title: Hyundai G4LC Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Oil Consumption - connecting rod and piston group wear
items.whatHappens: The G4LC was lightened by 14 kg compared to its predecessor, the G4FA. This weight reduction, combined with the aluminium block and cast iron liners, can lead to wear of the connecting rod and piston group over time. Owners report oil consumption that often goes unnoticed until it begins affecting the engine's mechanical integrity. Regular oil level checks are essential - the engine holds approximately 3.7-3.8 litres of oil.
items.repairVsReplace: On early-stage oil consumption, a top-end rebuild with new piston rings may resolve the issue. However, once bore scoring is present, the aluminium block cannot be overbored - full engine replacement is the only option.

items.title: Timing chain noise - cold-start rattle
items.whatHappens: The G4LC uses a simple leaf-type timing chain. While the engine's modest power output means the chain typically has a decent service life, active drivers who frequently rev the engine can experience chain stretch. Cold-start noise is the primary warning sign. The engine lacks hydraulic valve lifters - valve clearance should be checked approximately every 100,000 km (60,000 miles).
items.repairVsReplace: Timing chain replacement is a standard repair (£800-£1,500) and should be addressed promptly. If ignored, chain stretch can lead to timing jump and catastrophic valve/piston contact - at which point full engine replacement becomes the only viable option.

items.title: Overheating and cooling system issues
items.onset: Variable - often linked to urban driving patterns
items.whatHappens: The G4LC's lightweight aluminium block is susceptible to overheating damage. The modest water pump lifespan is a known concern, and short urban journeys - where the engine rarely reaches full operating temperature - accelerate wear. Even minor overheating can have significant consequences due to the engine's compact, lightened design.
items.repairVsReplace: Cooling system repairs (water pump: £300-£600) are straightforward. However, if overheating has caused warping or bore damage, replacement is the only option - the aluminium block cannot be reliably repaired once distorted.

failures.goodYearsLine: The G4LC was designed with meaningful improvements over the problematic G4FA - including piston cooling oil nozzles and a redesigned exhaust manifold to prevent catalyst debris entering the cylinders. Engines maintained with correct 0W-30 or 5W-30 specification oil and regular servicing typically exceed 200,000 km (≈124,000 miles), with some examples reaching 300,000 km (≈186,000 miles).

variants.title: How to Confirm You Have the G4LC
variants.intro: The G4LC is a specific engine code within the Hyundai-Kia Kappa II family. Unlike some engines with numerous sub-code variants, the G4LC is relatively consistent across applications - but confirming your exact code is still essential before ordering a replacement. Where to find your engine code: - On the engine: Stamped on a flat machined surface on the cylinder block, typically near the transmission bell housing on the front or side of the block - On the V5C registration document: Listed under vehicle details - Via VIN: Use an online decoder with your 17-character VIN Commonly confused codes - check you have the right one: - G4FA - 1.4-litre Gamma series (older generation, 2006-2018). The G4FA is the direct predecessor to the G4LC. The G4LC was redesigned with piston cooling oil nozzles and a revised exhaust manifold to fix the G4FA's well-documented catalyst disintegration problem. They are NOT interchangeable. - G4FC - 1.6-litre Gamma series. Physically very similar but has a larger bore and different stroke. Not interchangeable with the G4LC. - G4LA - 1.4-litre Kappa I (earlier generation). The G4LC is the Kappa II evolution; parts and ECU calibrations differ. Why getting the right code matters: The G4LC's aluminium block, revised oil system and different timing chain tensioner design mean that fitting a G4FA or G4FC into a G4LC-equipped car is not a straight swap - it requires different engine mounts, ECU calibration, and potentially different ancillaries. Always confirm your code before purchasing.

relatives.description: - the 1.4-litre Gamma series that preceded the G4LC. buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement G4LC - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: ** A used G4LC can be a sensible option for lower-value host vehicles (sub-£4,000 i20s or older Rios) - but only with documented service history and confirmation that the timing chain has been inspected. The G4LC's key weakness, oil consumption from piston/connecting rod wear, is not always visible on a low-mileage unit. Request a compression test and bore-scope inspection before committing to any used purchase. See used engine guide
options.href: /LINK PENDING - page not in current inventory

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: ** For most G4LC owners, a reconditioned unit is the sweet spot. A proper recon addresses the timing chain, tensioner, and any early-stage piston ring wear. Crucially, a reputable recon includes a full gasket set and new oil pump - exactly the components that fail first on this engine. With a 12-24 month warranty, this is the low-risk option for vehicles worth £5,000+. See reconditioned engine guide
options.href: /LINK PENDING - page not in current inventory

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: ** A full rebuild of the G4LC is only justified for high-value examples (low-mileage Konas, well-specced i30s) where the vehicle's value comfortably exceeds the rebuild cost. A quality rebuild should include new pistons, rings, bearings, timing components, and a full cylinder bore assessment. Given the aluminium block cannot be overbored if scored, confirm that the rebuilder has inspected the bores before committing - some "rebuilds" are simply reconditioned units with new gaskets. See rebuilt engine guide
options.href: /LINK PENDING - page not in current inventory

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: ** All replacement options can be supplied and fitted through our network of vetted UK Hyundai-Kia specialists - with warranties that follow the engine, not just the car. See supply & fit
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: ** The G4LC typically sits in vehicles worth £4,000-£16,000 (i20, i30, Kona, Rio, Ceed). A reconditioned G4LC at £1,450-£2,200 represents 10-55% of vehicle value - generally viable for most examples. However, for sub-£3,000 examples with high mileage and multiple existing faults, a used engine from £900-£1,200 is the more financially sensible route. Always evaluate the rest of the vehicle before committing to a reconditioned unit - a £2,000 engine in a £3,000 car with a failing clutch and worn suspension is rarely the right decision.

items.question: What are the most common problems with the G4LC engine?
items.answer: The G4LC's most documented issues are: (1) oil consumption from connecting rod and piston group wear, typically from 150,000 km (≈93,000 miles); (2) timing chain noise - a cold-start rattle that signals chain stretch; (3) cooling system failures - the lightweight aluminium block and modest water pump are sensitive to overheating, especially in urban driving. Oil consumption can lead to bore scoring - the aluminium block cannot be overbored; replacement is the only fix. Timing chain inspection is recommended at 100,000 km (60,000 miles). Regular oil changes with 0W-30 or 5W-30 specification are critical.

items.question: Which Hyundai and Kia models use the G4LC engine?
items.answer: The G4LC was fitted to: Hyundai - i20 (GB, BC3), i30 (GD, PD), Accent (RB, YC), Kona (OS), Venue, Solaris (HC). Kia - Rio (FB/YB, 4th gen), Ceed (JD, CD), Stonic (YB), Venga (YN). The engine entered production in 2014 and remains current in many markets. Power output is 100 hp @ 6,000 rpm and 133-134 Nm torque. The G4LC replaced the G4FA from 2014 onward. Check the engine code stamp on the cylinder block near the transmission bell housing.

items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned G4LC engine?
items.answer: For the G4LC, reconditioned is generally the smarter choice because the engine's key failure - bore wear - is often invisible on a used unit without a borescope inspection. However, for lower-value vehicles (sub-£4,000), a used engine from £900-£1,200 with documented chain service and compression test results can be viable. Used units risk hidden oil consumption and bore damage. Reconditioned units include new timing components, piston rings (where required), and a warranty. Rebuilt is only justified for high-value examples (low-mileage Konas, i30s) where the car's value exceeds the rebuild cost.

items.question: How do I know if my car has the G4LC engine and not another variant?
items.answer: The G4LC engine code is stamped on the cylinder block - look for a flat machined surface near the transmission bell housing, typically on the front or side of the block. The code also appears on the V5C registration document and can be confirmed via the vehicle's VIN using an online decoder. The G4LC is a 1.4-litre (1,368 cc) naturally aspirated petrol engine with MPI (multi-port injection). It is often confused with the G4FA (Gamma 1.4) or G4FC (Gamma 1.6) - physically similar but not interchangeable. Fitting a different code requires different engine mounts, ECU calibration, and ancillaries.

items.question: How long does a G4LC engine last?
items.answer: With proper maintenance, the G4LC can exceed 200,000 km (≈124,000 miles) and some well-maintained examples have reached 300,000 km (≈186,000 miles). The engine's longevity is highly dependent on oil change frequency - the recommended interval is 10,000 km (6,000 miles) or annually, whichever comes first. Use the correct 0W-30 or 5W-30 specification oil. The timing chain should be inspected at 100,000 km and replaced if noise or stretch is detected. Avoid repeated short urban trips - they prevent the engine from reaching full operating temperature, accelerating wear.
